newsitem.title: MEXICO: Analysts wary of Penoles Peru mine retreat.
newsitem.headline: Analysts wary of Penoles Peru mine retreat.

text.p: Flabbergasted analysts on Friday disagreed over whether Mexico silver giant Penoles will suffer from its surprise decision to back out of the privatization of a stake in Peruvian mine La Oroya.

Analysts said they were still in shock over Penoles' abrupt decision to quit the project, which they were still lauding just last week. Two months ago the company agreed to purchase a 60 percent stake of the metallurgic complex for a total $227 million.
On Thursday the company said, "The requirements...to guarantee adequate profitability did not come together," in a reference to negotiations with Peru's state mining company Centromin.

But after having hyped the project and persuaded wary analysts it could resolve environmental problems, tackle heavy sulfuric dioxide emissions and improve the productivity of its hefty workforce, Penoles appeared to have changed its mind.
"It's disappointing that they are walking away from something that wouldn't have been so difficult to turn around and make world-competitive," Paribas' London-based analyst Nigel Kieser said.
He dropped his recommendation on the stock to sell from buy after Penoles' decision.
"After all the patience it took to finally get part of Centromin, it is hard to believe Penoles is walking away so soon," Valores Finamex analyst Chris Albi wrote in a report.
"Penoles should have known exactly what it was getting into at the time of the auction."
At least one analyst said good riddance to La Oroya, and that Penoles could be better off without the complex.

"I don't think investors should be broken-hearted -- they weren't going to make a lot of money on this. Penoles has got a lot on its plate and is not begging for new projects," Kleinwort Benson analyst Warwick Jones said.
The company would not provide more details on its decision, but said it would continue to bid for project in Peru and the rest of Latin America.
"I have a feeling the issues that caused the problems were related to social and environmental responsibilities," Kieser said.
Clean-up from years of environmental plunder could reach $130 million, Keiser said. The Peruvian government agreed to foot the bill, but may have later asked Penoles to contribute, he added.
Centromin said the decision to back out was "a shame," but said Penoles would be welcome to bid for other auctions, after it pays a $1 million fine.
Some analysts said the company could use the $380 million loan it recently secured to invest in other projects it is eyeing and for development in Mexico.
But Penoles' image in such auctions could be tarnished from its eleventh hour retreat in Peru.
"The impact on Penoles' reputation depends on why they pulled out, if they were asking too much and being unrealistic," Kieser said.
Penoles shares dropped 0.80 pesos or 2.3 percent on Thursday after the news. On Friday they fell another 0.90 pesos, trading at 33 pesos per share early in the session.
